summary: Describes the syntax and procedures for computing and verifying digital signatures in version 1.0 of the Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP). Signatures let parties in a trade check who sent a message and that it was not altered. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2802 describes how Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) version 1.0 messages, written in Extensible Markup Language (XML), can include digital signatures. A signature identifies the information being protected and provides a value that a recipient can verify.

questions: what is the iotp signature manifest
subtitle: The XML signature syntax and procedures specified for Internet Open Trading Protocol version 1.0.

tldr.problem: IOTP messages are XML documents, and parts of those messages need authentication and integrity protection even when the payment system has its own security.
tldr.mechanism: A Signature contains a Manifest with digests, references, originator and recipient information, and algorithms. The Manifest is canonicalized and digested, then the digest is signed or authenticated.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2802 defines syntax and procedures for digital signatures in IOTP version 1.0. It is Informational and does not define general XML signature syntax for all applications.

today: RFC 2802 is an Informational memo describing signature syntax for IOTP version 1.0. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Purpose and Requirements
sections.content:
The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) provides a payment-system-independent framework for Internet commerce, and its messages are XML documents. Although IOTP assumes that a payment system provides security, some parts of IOTP messages still need authentication and integrity protection.

This memo proposes signature syntax and procedures for IOTP version 1.0. It aims to authenticate transactions, make tampering detectable, support multiple algorithms and keep signatures lightweight. It anticipates that future IOTP versions may adopt a general XML signature effort.
sections.plainLanguage: IOTP uses XML to carry information for online commerce. This memo explains how version 1.0 messages can identify their signer and reveal changes to signed information.

sections.title: Signature, Manifest and Digests
sections.content:
An IOTP Signature has a Manifest and one or more signature Values. The Manifest is the authenticated part: it lists digests and references to resources, identifies the originator and recipient, names algorithms and may include additional attributes.

A Digest combines a locator for a resource with the digest value. The signature is indirect: it is calculated over the Manifest, which contains the references and digests, rather than directly over every resource. OriginatorInfo is required; RecipientInfo can identify a particular recipient or supply information used to determine the authentication key.
sections.plainLanguage: The Manifest lists what information the signature covers, which algorithms are used and who is involved. The signature value protects that Manifest, which in turn contains digests of the referenced information.

sections.title: Computing and Verifying a Signature
sections.content:
To create a signature, the Manifest is first canonicalized so that whitespace differences introduced by XML parsing do not change its representation. A digest algorithm then produces a value from the canonical form. Finally, a signature algorithm signs or authenticates that digest, and the result is placed in a Value element.

The Manifest contains identifiers that let other elements refer to algorithm definitions and digest values. A critical Attribute that a recipient does not recognize requires rejection of the signature; an unrecognized non-critical attribute may be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender puts the Manifest into a consistent form, calculates its digest and creates a signature value from that digest. The recipient can repeat the digest step and check the signature against it.

sections.title: Supported Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC says IOTP version 1.0 requires DSA, DOM-HASH, SHA1 and HMAC implementations; RSA implementation is recommended. SHA1 produces a 160-bit digest. DOM-HASH computes a digest based on the XML document's DOM representation and may use SHA1.

The RFC uses the word digital signature for both public-key signatures and message authentication codes. DSA and RSA are public-key algorithms; HMAC uses a shared secret. ECDSA is also described, but it is not among the listed mandatory algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes several ways to produce a signature value. Some use public and private keys; HMAC instead uses a shared secret between the parties.

sections.title: XML Components and Certificates
sections.content:
The top-level IotpSignatures element contains one or more Signature elements and may contain certificates. A Signature contains a Manifest and one or more Values. Values are base64 encoded by default, though the format can specify no encoding.

A Certificate can carry a certificate value or a locator to retrieve it. If the Certificate element is used, support for X.509 version 3 certificates is mandatory in this specification. The security section refers readers to RFC 2801 for IOTP security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The XML structure separates the information being signed from the signature value. A certificate can be included in the message or identified by a link.
